doctrines/christology/question: If Jesus Christ is truly God, how is he also truly human — and how are deity and humanity united in one Christ?
doctrines/christology/summary: Once Nicaea confessed the Son fully God, the question became how God the Word is also a real man. Docetists denied a real body; adoptionists denied real deity; Apollinaris denied a human mind; the Antiochene school stressed two complete natures, the Alexandrian school one incarnate Word. Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451) produced the formula ‘one person in two natures’ — and three lasting communions: Chalcedonian (Orthodox, Catholic, Protestant), Miaphysite (Oriental Orthodox) and East Syriac (Church of the East). Later debates concerned Christ's wills (681), his self-emptying (kenotic Christology) and whether he could have sinned.
doctrines/christology/longText:
The earliest Christological controversies concerned Christ's humanity, not his deity. Ignatius of Antioch (c. 110) wrote against those who said Christ ‘only seemed to suffer’ (Greek dokein, hence docetism), and the Johannine letters insist that ‘Jesus Christ is come in the flesh’ (1 John 4:2). Gnostic and Marcionite teachers distinguished the heavenly Christ from the man Jesus or denied his birth. At the other pole, Ebionites and later adoptionists held that Jesus was a man chosen and filled with God's power.

After Nicaea, the issue sharpened. Apollinaris of Laodicea, a staunch Nicene, proposed that in Christ the divine Word took the place of the human rational soul — guaranteeing a single, sinless subject. Gregory of Nazianzus replied with a principle that governed all later Christology: ‘that which He has not assumed He has not healed’. Apollinarianism was condemned at Constantinople (381).

Two schools then clashed. Antiochene theologians (Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore of Mopsuestia, Nestorius) stressed the full humanity of Jesus — his growth, temptation, and obedience — and spoke of the Word dwelling in the man as in a temple, joined in one prosopon (presentation). Alexandrian theologians (Athanasius, Cyril) stressed that the one subject of every act of Christ is God the Word himself, who ‘became flesh’. When Nestorius, archbishop of Constantinople, objected to calling Mary Theotokos (‘God-bearer’), preferring Christotokos, Cyril of Alexandria led the opposition. The Council of Ephesus (431) deposed Nestorius and affirmed Theotokos; the Formula of Reunion (433) reconciled Cyril with the Antiochenes.

The Archimandrite Eutyches then taught that after the union Christ's humanity was not consubstantial with ours. The ‘Robber Synod’ of Ephesus (449) vindicated him; Pope Leo I's Tome insisted on two natures each acting in communion with the other. The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as ‘one and the same… acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation’. For Rome and Constantinople this balanced Cyril and Leo; for many in Egypt, Syria and Armenia, ‘in two natures’ sounded Nestorian and betrayed Cyril's ‘one incarnate nature of God the Word’. The Miaphysite churches — Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, Syriac, later Malankara — separated over the following century. The Church of the East in Persia, already independent and honouring Theodore, formally adopted a dyophysite Christology at synods in 484–486 and later (Babai the Great) of two natures and two qnome in one parsopa.

Imperial attempts at reunion — the Henotikon (482), Justinian's condemnation of the ‘Three Chapters’ at Constantinople II (553), and Heraclius' monoenergism and monothelitism (‘one will’) — failed. Maximus the Confessor, mutilated for his resistance, argued that a complete human nature must have a human will; the Third Council of Constantinople (681) defined two wills and two energies harmoniously united.

Modern Christology has asked new questions. Lutheran and Anglican ‘kenotic’ theologians (Thomasius, Gore) proposed that the Word laid aside divine attributes such as omniscience in becoming man (Philippians 2:7). Liberal theologians (Schleiermacher, Ritschl) built Christology ‘from below’, beginning with the historical Jesus. Evangelical and Reformed theologians debate whether Christ was impeccable (unable to sin) or only sinless. Ecumenically, the late 20th century brought remarkable rapprochement: Catholic and Oriental Orthodox declarations (1971, 1973, 1984), the Orthodox–Oriental Orthodox agreed statements (1989–90), and the Catholic–Assyrian Common Christological Declaration (1994) concluded that the 5th-century divisions were largely about terminology.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/0/label: How is Christ both truly God and truly human — and one?
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/0/text: After Nicaea settled that the Son is fully God, the question became how God the Word is also a complete human being without becoming two Christs.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/1/label: Phil 2:6–8 — ‘emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/1/text: The kenosis hymn: basic for every view of how the divine Son became human; central to modern kenotic Christology.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/2/label: Heb 2:17; 4:15 — ‘in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin’
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/2/text: Full humanity, real temptation and sinlessness — the root of the impeccability debate.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/3/label: Matt 26:39 — ‘not as I will, but as thou wilt’
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/3/text: Gethsemane: the key text in the monothelite controversy over Christ's human will.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/4/label: Luke 2:52; Mark 13:32 — ‘increased in wisdom’; ‘neither the Son’
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/4/text: Growth and limited knowledge: Antiochene evidence for a full human mind; kenotic evidence for self-limitation.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/5/label: John 1:14; 1 John 4:2 — ‘the Word was made flesh’
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/5/text: The Alexandrian keystone: the Word himself became flesh. The Johannine letters already oppose those who deny Christ ‘come in the flesh’.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/6/text: Spiritual Christ, phantom body; found among Gnostics and Marcion.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/7/label: Adoptionism: a man adopted as Son
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/7/text: Ebionites, Theodotus, Paul of Samosata; revived in 8th-century Spain.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/8/label: Ignatius: ‘God existing in flesh’ — truly born, truly suffered
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/8/text: On the road to martyrdom in Rome, Ignatius insists the reality of Christ's flesh is the basis of the Eucharist and of his own suffering.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/9/label: Irenaeus: he became what we are
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/9/text: Recapitulation: Christ sums up and heals human life by living it in full.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/10/labe: Apollinaris: the Word replaces the human mind
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/10/text: One divine subject, one nature; no human rational soul in Christ.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/11/labe: Gregory: ‘that which He has not assumed He has not healed’
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/11/text: If Christ lacked a human mind, the human mind — the seat of sin — is not redeemed.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/12/text: The council anathematises the Apollinarians among others.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/13/labe: Antioch: Theodore of Mopsuestia — two complete natures
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/13/text: The Word indwells the assumed man ‘by good pleasure’; strong emphasis on Christ's human moral struggle.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/14/text: Nestorius objects to calling Mary ‘Mother of God’; opponents accuse him of teaching two sons.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/15/labe: Cyril: one incarnate Word; Mary is Theotokos
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/15/text: The single subject of Christ's acts and sufferings is God the Word; the Twelve Anathemas.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/16/text: Theotokos affirmed; rival Antiochene council; reconciled by the Formula of Reunion (433).
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/17/labe: Church of the East adopts dyophysite Christology
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/17/text: Synods of Beth Lapat (484) and Seleucia-Ctesiphon (486); the School of Edessa moves to Nisibis; the East Syriac church spreads to India, Central Asia and China.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/18/text: Two natures before the union, one after; Christ's body not consubstantial with ours.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/19/text: Under Dioscorus of Alexandria; Flavian of Constantinople is deposed and dies; Leo calls it a latrocinium.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/20/labe: Leo's Tome: each nature acts in communion with the other
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/20/text: Two natures, one person; the Word does what belongs to the Word, the flesh what belongs to the flesh.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/21/labe: Council of Chalcedon: one person ‘in two natures’
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/21/text: Without confusion, change, division or separation. Dioscorus deposed.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/22/text: Received by Rome, Constantinople and later the Protestant churches.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/23/text: Cyril's ‘one incarnate nature of God the Word’; rejects both Eutyches and Chalcedon. Severus of Antioch its great theologian.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/24/text: Henotikon (482) fails; Severus exiled (518); Jacob Baradaeus ordains a parallel hierarchy (from 542). Egypt, Ethiopia, Armenia, much of Syria remain non-Chalcedonian.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/25/text: Justinian reads Chalcedon in a Cyrilline (‘Neo-Chalcedonian’) sense, condemning Theodore of Mopsuestia, to win back Miaphysites. It does not.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/26/text: Patriarch Sergius and Emperor Heraclius' compromise: two natures, one divine-human operation and will (Ekthesis, 638).
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/27/labe: Maximus the Confessor: a full humanity needs a human will
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/27/text: In Gethsemane the human will freely submits to the divine. Maximus' tongue and right hand were cut off (662).
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/28/labe: Constantinople III: two wills, two energies
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/28/text: The human will follows the divine without resistance; Pope Honorius I posthumously condemned.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/29/text: Christ's divinity as the perfect strength of his God-consciousness.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/30/text: Thomasius (1853), Gore (1889–91), P. T. Forsyth: the Son lays aside or limits divine attributes in becoming man.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/31/labe: Could Christ have sinned? Impeccability vs peccability
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/31/text: Edward Irving's teaching that Christ took fallen flesh (deposed 1833) and later evangelical debate (Hodge vs Shedd).
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/32/text: Anba Bishoy (1989) and Chambésy (1990): both families share the same faith expressed in different terms; Catholic–Coptic (1973) and Catholic–Syriac (1984) declarations.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/33/text: John Paul II and Mar Dinkha IV: divisions due largely to misunderstanding; the Assyrian Church may call Mary ‘Mother of Christ our God and Saviour’.
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/34/labe: Today: three Christological families in growing dialogue
doctrines/christology/flow/nodes/34/text: Chalcedonians (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, most Protestants), Miaphysites (c. 60 million Oriental Orthodox, largely in Ethiopia, Egypt, Armenia, India, Syria) and the Assyrian/East Syriac churches; full communion not yet restored.
doctrines/scripture-authority/question: Which books are Scripture, and where does final authority for Christian belief lie — in Scripture alone, in Scripture with Tradition, in the Church's teaching office, or with reason and experience alongside?
doctrines/scripture-authority/summary: The early church received Israel's Scriptures and gradually recognised a New Testament against Marcion and the Gnostics, guided by apostolic origin, orthodoxy and catholic use. Canon lists (Muratorian fragment, Athanasius 367, Carthage 397) converged on 27 New Testament books, but Old Testament canons still differ: Protestant 66, Catholic 73, Orthodox larger, Ethiopian 81. The deeper question — how Scripture relates to Tradition, councils, bishops and popes — divided Reformation churches (sola scriptura) from Trent, shaped Vatican I's definition of papal infallibility (1870), and continues in debates over inerrancy, higher criticism, and Wesleyan, Pentecostal and global-South approaches.
doctrines/scripture-authority/longText:
Jesus and the apostles appealed to ‘the scriptures’ — the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (Luke 24:44) — usually in the Greek Septuagint, which included books later called deuterocanonical or apocryphal. Alongside them, the churches read the apostles' letters and the Gospels; 2 Peter 3:16 already counts Paul's letters with ‘the other scriptures’. In the second century, Marcion of Sinope rejected the Old Testament and published a canon of an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters; Gnostic teachers produced new gospels. In response, Irenaeus defended a fourfold Gospel, the ‘rule of faith’ and succession of bishops from the apostles as public tests of truth.

The New Testament canon took shape through use more than decree. The Muratorian fragment (traditionally c. 170–200; some scholars date it to the 4th century) lists most of our books. Eusebius (c. 325) sorted books into acknowledged, disputed and spurious. Athanasius' 39th Festal Letter (367) is the first list of exactly our 27 books; North African councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) agreed, and Pope Innocent I (405) concurred. Jerome, translating the Vulgate from Hebrew, regarded books outside the Hebrew canon as ecclesiastical rather than canonical; Augustine accepted the broader Septuagint collection. Eastern churches long hesitated over Revelation; the Syriac Peshitta omitted 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation; the Ethiopian church developed the largest canon, including Enoch and Jubilees.

The Reformation turned the question of canon into a question of authority. Luther at Worms (1521) refused to recant unless convinced ‘by Scripture and plain reason’; the Reformers held that Scripture is the supreme, sufficient and self-interpreting norm (sola scriptura), with creeds and councils as subordinate standards. They followed Jerome in placing the Apocrypha in a separate section — useful but not doctrinally authoritative — later omitted from many Protestant Bibles. The Council of Trent (1546) responded by defining the larger canon and declaring that saving truth is contained ‘in the written books and the unwritten traditions’, to be received with equal reverence, interpreted by the Church. Radical reformers and Quakers emphasised the inner Word or Light; Anglicans appealed to Scripture, the early Fathers and reason; John Wesley, a ‘man of one book’, also drew on tradition, reason and experience — a pattern later called the Wesleyan quadrilateral.

The nineteenth century brought historical criticism (Strauss, Wellhausen), which read the Bible as a collection of human documents with complex histories, and responses ranging from liberal accommodation to the Princeton doctrine of inerrancy (Hodge and Warfield, 1881) and the later fundamentalist movement. In 1870 the First Vatican Council defined that the pope, speaking ex cathedra on faith and morals, is preserved from error — a decision opposed by a minority and leading to the Old Catholic schism. Eastern Orthodox theologians present Scripture as the heart of Holy Tradition, guarded by the whole conciliar Church rather than by a single office.

The twentieth century added neo-orthodoxy (Barth: Scripture as witness to the Word of God), Vatican II's Dei Verbum (1965: Scripture and Tradition flowing from the same divine wellspring), the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) and evangelical debates over limited inerrancy, alongside Pentecostal and global-South readings in which Scripture is read with expectation of present prophetic power. All Christian traditions treat Scripture as uniquely authoritative; they disagree about its extent, its interpreter and its relation to the living church.
doctrines/scripture-authority/flow/nodes: Which books are Scripture — and who or what has final authority to interpret them?
Two linked questions: the extent of the canon, and the relation of Scripture to tradition, church office, reason and experience.
2 Thess 2:15 — ‘hold the traditions… whether by word, or our epistle’
Apostolic tradition in both oral and written form; a key text for Catholics and Orthodox.
2 Tim 3:15–17 — ‘All scripture is given by inspiration of God’
Inspiration and sufficiency for teaching; the classic proof-text for sola scriptura and inerrancy.
Mark 7:8–13 — ‘the tradition of men’
Jesus criticises traditions that nullify God's word; cited by Reformers against human traditions.
Matt 16:18–19 — ‘thou art Peter, and upon this rock’
The keys given to Peter: foundation of Catholic claims for papal primacy; read by others of Peter's confession or of all apostles.
Luke 24:44 — ‘the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms’
A three-part Jewish Scripture, the background for later debates about the Old Testament canon and the Septuagint.
2 Pet 1:20–21; 3:16 — Paul's letters among ‘the other scriptures’
Prophecy not of private interpretation; Paul's letters already counted as Scripture.
Marcion's canon: edited Luke + ten Pauline letters
The first known closed Christian canon, rejecting the Old Testament and its God.
Irenaeus: four Gospels, rule of faith, apostolic succession
Public, apostolic tradition in the churches, especially Rome, against secret Gnostic tradition.
Muratorian fragment: an early list of New Testament books
Accepts four Gospels, Acts, thirteen Pauline letters, Jude, two letters of John, Revelation and the Wisdom of Solomon; Hermas allowed to be read privately. Dating debated.
Athanasius' 39th Festal Letter: the 27 books
First list identical to the modern New Testament; Old Testament close to the Hebrew canon plus Baruch, with Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit ‘to be read’.
Basil: written and unwritten apostolic tradition
Some practices come from Scripture, others from unwritten tradition; both have the same force.
Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) list the canon
African councils list the broader Old Testament (with Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Maccabees) and the 27 New Testament books.
Augustine: the Church's authority moves me to believe the Gospel
Scripture is supreme, but its recognition is bound up with the catholic Church.
Jerome: ‘Hebrew verity’ and the Apocrypha
Vulgate translator who distinguished canonical (Hebrew) books from those read for edification.
Vincent of Lérins: everywhere, always, by all
Scripture is sufficient, but must be interpreted by the catholic consensus.
Ethiopian canon: 81 books including Enoch and Jubilees
Ge'ez translation from the 5th–6th centuries; the broadest canon in Christianity.
Papal supremacy claims grow (Gregory VII to Boniface VIII)
Dictatus papae (1075), Unam Sanctam (1302): the Roman pontiff as supreme judge in the Church.
Conciliarism: a general council above the pope
The Council of Constance ends the Western Schism and declares (Haec Sancta) that councils hold power directly from Christ.
Sola scriptura: Luther at Worms
Conscience captive to the Word of God; popes and councils can err.
Protestant canon: 66 books; Apocrypha set apart
Luther's Bible (1534) prints the Apocrypha separately; Westminster (1647) excludes it from the canon.
Council of Trent: canon defined; Scripture and unwritten traditions
Session IV (8 April 1546) defines 73 books and the Vulgate as authentic; the Church interprets Scripture.
Catholic: Scripture and Tradition under the Magisterium
One deposit of faith in two modes, authentically interpreted by the bishops in communion with the pope.
Quakers: the Inner Light
George Fox: Christ speaks directly to the soul; Scripture is a secondary rule.
Wesley: Scripture, tradition, reason, experience
‘A man of one book’ who also appealed to the early church, reason and experience.
Historical (higher) criticism
Strauss' Life of Jesus (1835), Wellhausen's Prolegomena (1878): the Bible as historically developed human literature.
Vatican I: papal infallibility defined
Pastor Aeternus: ex cathedra definitions are irreformable of themselves; opposition leads to the Old Catholic churches.
Inerrancy: Princeton theology
Hodge and Warfield: Scripture is without error in the original autographs.
Barth: the threefold Word of God
Jesus Christ is the Word; Scripture witnesses to him and becomes God's Word in the event of revelation.
Vatican II, Dei Verbum
Scripture and Tradition flow from the same divine wellspring; the Magisterium is not above the Word of God but serves it.
Infallibility of purpose / limited inerrancy
Scripture is fully trustworthy in what it intends to teach about salvation and faith, not necessarily in incidental science or history.
Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy
Nearly 300 evangelical leaders affirm inerrancy in nineteen articles; the Southern Baptist ‘conservative resurgence’ follows (from 1979).
Orthodox: Scripture within Holy Tradition
The Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848): the guardian of faith is the whole people of God; councils express the Church's mind.
Global South: Bible-centred, Spirit-expectant reading
African, Asian and Latin American churches often read Scripture as directly applicable to healing, spiritual powers and justice; translation into thousands of languages shapes local theology.
Today: shared Scriptures, different canons and interpreters

All traditions share the 27-book New Testament; Old Testament canons still differ. The magisterium, conciliarity, sola scriptura, inerrancy and critical scholarship remain live fault-lines and dialogue topics.
